summary: Suggests a schedule for implementing the IP network number allocation plan described in RFC 1366. It was replaced by RFC 1467.

plainLanguage.summary: A timeline that says when each step of the new address handing-out plan should happen.

subtitle: A timeline for rolling out new Internet address allocation rules.

tldr.problem: The Internet was running out of unallocated Class B addresses, threatening the viability of routing tables and address space management. RFC 1366 proposed new allocation guidelines; a realistic implementation schedule was needed.
tldr.mechanism: Define four milestones between October 1992 and June 1993 to gradually restrict Class B issuance and move to block-based Class C allocation, allowing time for preparation of address aggregation mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The schedule helped the Internet community prepare for the transition to classless interdomain routing (CIDR). This document was replaced by RFC 1467.

today: RFC 1367 is informational and was replaced by RFC 1467. This schedule from 1992 outlined the transition to CIDR, which successfully prevented Internet routing collapse.

sections.title: The Address Crisis
sections.content:
By 1992, the Internet's address space allocation system was straining. Class A addresses were essentially unavailable, Class B addresses were depleting rapidly, and the resulting large number of routing table entries threatened the Internet's routing infrastructure. RFC 1366 proposed new guidelines for managing IP address allocation, including moving toward block allocation of Class C addresses and developing address aggregation mechanisms to reduce routing table size.

This RFC proposes a realistic schedule for implementing those guidelines. It was drafted by the Federal Networking Council Engineering and Planning Group based on discussions with IANA, the Internet Registry, and the broader Internet community, with the assumption that address aggregation mechanisms would be available by mid-1993.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet ran out of big address blocks. New rules were needed for handing them out more carefully. This says when each step would happen.

sections.title: Early Phases
sections.content:
Phase 1 (October 31, 1992): Regional address registry criteria take effect. Class A remains unavailable. Class B allocation continues only when justified, with preference for blocks of Class C addresses instead. Class C allocation follows the new plan, administered by the Internet Registry or regional registries.

Phase 2 (February 14, 1993): Re-evaluation of the schedule if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: October 1992: start saying no to Class B. February: check if the plan is working.

sections.title: Transition to Block Allocation
sections.content:
Phase 3 (April 15, 1993): The Internet Registry begins allocating all networks in appropriately sized blocks of Class C numbers according to the addressing plan. Class B becomes difficult to obtain and is issued only when carefully justified.

Phase 4 (June 6, 1993): Address aggregation mechanisms are expected to be available in the Internet, allowing the transition to Classless Interdomain Routing (CIDR). This endpoint of the schedule represents the moment when the Internet's routing infrastructure could reliably use CIDR to compress routing tables and prevent the exhaustion of router memory.
sections.plainLanguage: April 1993: fully switch to giving out Class C blocks. June: the new routing system (CIDR) is ready.

references.text: Gerich, E., "Guidelines for Management of IP Address Space", RFC 1366, October 1992.
